title: A Measurement of Home
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 41 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
The first time the Brasswatch Door jammed after Threadrain, Danse accused the hinge.

The hinge, which was an inanimate piece of brass, had no opportunity to defend itself.

“Manufacturing defect,” he said.

“You made it,” I reminded him.

He stared at me.

“Your point?”

“My point is I'm choosing my next words very carefully.”

He looked back at the door, which had stopped halfway open between the repair yard and the Commonwealth. Beyond it, the wind carried dry dust and a smell of hot metal. On our side, cold droplets slid down the frame even though the morning sky was clear.

Danse had drawn three lines in chalk on the ground.

He had also placed a safety barrier made from two crates and a plank. It looked incredibly official for an object that would collapse if somebody leaned on it.

“I want to check the lower bracket,” I said.

“The lower bracket is secure.”

“It was secure yesterday.”

He folded his arms.

“Did you come here to assist?”

“Yes.”

“Then assist.”

“I am. I'm trying to stop you from declaring victory before you measure the problem.”

A voice came from behind us.

“That's what I've been telling him.”

Toph Beifong stood at the edge of the yard with one foot against the stone path and a grin that suggested she was enjoying the conversation far too much.

Danse looked heavenward.

“I was informed you would arrive at noon.”

“Lucky for you, I got bored early.”

She moved toward the door without hesitation. Danse stepped aside at once, despite looking as though he hated doing it.

Toph set her hand against the wall, then placed her bare foot on the stone.

“The hinge is fine,” she said.

Danse made a small, strangled sound.

“The frame's twisting.”

“That is impossible. The base is reinforced.”

“Sure is. The ground beneath it isn't.”

I crouched to study the chalk lines. The left line had shifted less than the width of a finger. It was enough.

“Threadrain washed out the foundation,” I said.

Danse stared at the door.

“Then the hinge is suffering a secondary alignment failure.”

“You can say Toph was right,” I said.

“I can say the hinge is not the primary problem.”

“Beautiful. We're making progress.”

Toph laughed.

For the next two hours we argued over how to keep the doorway safe while rebuilding its footing. Danse wanted temporary braces, then an inspection. Toph wanted the dirt removed before anyone even considered tightening the supports. I wanted everyone to stop standing in the puddle beneath the electrical junction.

“Why?” Danse asked.

I pointed to the exposed wire.

He looked at it, then stepped backward.

“Valid concern.”

“Mark the date,” Toph said. “He learned something from a civilian.”

“I'm not going to survive you two,” Danse muttered.

“Probably not,” I said. “But your hinge will.”

The danger came at midday.

A young volunteer from the kitchen attempted to move one of our tool crates around the safety barrier. The ground near the frame gave a soft crack. The crate slipped, and a dozen bolts clattered toward the opening.

“Back!” Danse shouted.

The volunteer stopped.

Toph stamped once and drew a ridge of stone up between the door and the falling crate. Danse reached forward, caught the crate by its handle, and pulled it away from the shifting edge.

Nobody fell. Nobody was injured.

It would have been an excellent moment for us to congratulate ourselves.

Instead Danse turned toward the volunteer.

“Why were you inside the barrier?”

“I thought I was helping.”

“You were told—”

“Danse,” I said.

He stopped speaking. His face had gone hard in the familiar way that came before an order he would later regret.

“The barrier is flimsy,” I said. “It didn't clearly show where the unsafe ground started. That was our mistake.”

“I should've asked,” the volunteer said.

“Yes,” Danse replied, after a moment. “You should have. And I should have marked the exclusion area properly.”

The kid blinked.

Danse looked at the crates with obvious dislike.

“We will fix that now.”

We did.

Toph raised a low stone border along the dangerous edge. I painted bright warning marks on scrap boards. Danse inspected every approach, then wrote SAFE WORKING AREA in block letters that could probably be read from another universe.

“Subtle,” I said.

“Clarity is not an artistic failure.”

“Greg would disagree.”

“He disagrees with my taste in music.”

“Your taste in music is marching songs.”

“Some marching songs are excellent.”

“Name one that you play for pleasure.”

He opened his mouth, thought about it, and changed the subject.

By late afternoon the repaired base held. Toph left with the promise to inspect it again after the next rain and an inexplicable amount of satisfaction about having insulted both our methods. Danse checked the alignment three times.

I let him.

When he finally closed the tool case, he looked tired in a way that wasn't simply physical.

“You were angry earlier,” I said.

“About what?”

“The volunteer. Your voice went somewhere familiar.”

His jaw tightened.

“I nearly let someone get hurt.”

“You did stop it.”

“I made an inadequate barrier.”

“Yes. You did.”

He blinked, apparently offended by my refusal to make the story nicer.

I continued. “And you corrected it. We can do both.”

He sat on the bench outside the workshop.

“I used to believe if I planned well enough, nothing would go wrong.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It was efficient.”

“It clearly wasn't. You just admitted things went wrong.”

A reluctant breath left him.

“Your logic is irritating.”

“That's why you keep me around.”

“That is not the only reason.”

I sat beside him. A gull cried somewhere beyond the Starwake path. It sounded nothing like Boston, and that sometimes made him turn his head as though checking whether he had woken in the wrong place.

“What are the other reasons?” I asked.

He studied his gloved hands.

“You tell me when I'm making a mistake,” he said. “You don't let me call a command a conversation. You remember that my choices belong to me.”

“Even the bad ones?”

“Especially those.”

I touched his sleeve. “Can we talk about the other conversation, too?”

He knew which one. The one we'd begun long before the Commonwealth workshop felt like home. The one about my polyamory, his uncertainty, and the difference between loving somebody and requiring their entire schedule.

“We can,” he said.

“I don't want the ease of our life here to become an excuse not to check in.”

He nodded slowly. “I need notice before plans change. Not permission requests. Notice. If it affects something we've arranged, I want to discuss it.”

“Fair.”

“And I won't pretend that something unfamiliar is a threat just because the rules I learned didn't cover it.”

I looked at him. “That took practice.”

“It did.”

“Are you comfortable?”

“Not in every situation.” He met my eyes. “But I know what I have agreed to, and I know I can talk to you if that changes.”

“That's what I need.”

He took off one glove and held out his hand. I placed mine in it.

The roughness of his palm was familiar now, as were the small cuts acquired from fixing things nobody paid him to fix. His thumb brushed the inside of my wrist.

“Would you stay for dinner?” he asked.

“Are you cooking?”

“Yes.”

“Then I have some safety concerns.”

He looked offended.

“Your last attempt was edible,” I said.

“High praise.”

“Not technically a compliment.”

“I'll take it.”

He leaned toward me and waited. I kissed him because I wanted to, because he wanted to, and because neither of us believed a kiss settled every future question. The warmth of his mouth and the smell of oil on his collar made me forget the door for an instant.

When we parted, he rested his forehead against mine.

“Dinner,” he reminded me.

“Right. The dangerous part.”

We went inside together and left the repaired door shut for the evening. Whatever the next storm brought, it could wait until morning.

The next morning, the threshold lamp stayed dry.

Three others did not.

Across Lanternwell Square, the public maintenance board showed two reports of the same damaged railing, each bearing a different name. Neri looked at the entries, then at the weather, and frowned.

“Something's being counted twice,” they said.

I thought of the missing tea, the shifted footing, and a doorway that had needed three different sets of eyes.

“Then we should count it together,” I said.

Danse picked up his notebook.

“Agreed.”

That was new, too.
